references.text: God promises Abraham a son through Sarah, emphasizing that nothing is impossible for God.
The Lord does as He has said; Sarah becomes pregnant and bears a son to Abraham in his old age, at the time God had specified.
Jeremiah confesses that the Lord has created heaven and earth and that nothing is too hard for Him—a direct parallel to the question in Gen 18:14.
The Lord asks: 'Is anything too hard for Me?'—using the same Hebrew expression (הֲיִפָּלֵא) as in Gen 18:14.
The Lord asks Moses if His arm is too short, showing that God's power has no limits.
The angel Gabriel tells Mary that nothing is impossible for God, a direct reflection of God's words to Abraham and Sarah.
Jesus says that for humans this is impossible, but for God all things are possible—the same principle of God's omnipotence.
By faith, Sarah received power to conceive even though she was past the age, because she considered Him faithful who had promised. The fulfillment of God's promise in Gen 18:14.
Direct quotation and theological confirmation of the promise concerning Isaac's birth at the appointed time.
Concrete fulfillment of the prophecy that Sarah will give birth at the appointed time, confirming God's faithfulness.
Sarah's own affirmation that what was humanly impossible was made possible by God, in response to the prophecy.
Repetition and confirmation of the prophecy concerning Isaac's birth at the precisely appointed time.
The direct fulfillment of the prophecy, confirming that God's promise is effective and kept at the appointed time.
Theological parallel: God's ability to give a child to a woman when her time has passed, in response to prayer and faith.
Typological parallel: God's ability to make the impossible possible through a supernatural birth, even though the context differs.
